subject: Architecture
title: Big Ben: The Clock That Named a Tower
description: A quick win: understand Big Ben: The Clock That Named a Tower.

hook.text: Big Ben is not the tower. It's the name of the 13-ton bell inside it.

buildup.text: The clock's four faces are 23 feet wide. The minute hands are 14 feet long.

discovery.text: The clock has kept accurate time since 1859, corrected by adding or removing old pennies from the pendulum.

twist.text: The first bell cracked during testing. It was recast, cracked again, and has chimed with that crack ever since.

climax.text: The tower's official name was changed to Elizabeth Tower in 2012, but nobody uses it.

punchline.text: A cracked bell with the wrong name. London wouldn't have it any other way.

quiz.question: What does the name 'Big Ben' actually refer to?

details.summary: Big Ben is actually the name of the 13.7-ton bell inside the Elizabeth Tower at London's Palace of Westminster. The clock mechanism, designed in 1859, keeps time accurate to within one second per day using a stack of old pennies on the pendulum to fine-tune its swing rate.
details.whyItMatters: Big Ben demonstrates that great engineering can be beautifully simple. Using pennies to adjust a massive clock's accuracy shows that elegant low-tech solutions can outperform complex alternatives, a principle relevant to every engineering discipline.
takeaways: Big Ben is the bell, not the tower (officially Elizabeth Tower)
The 1859 clock keeps time within one second per day
Old pennies on the pendulum fine-tune the swing rate

faq.question: How do pennies adjust the clock's accuracy?
faq.answer: Adding a penny raises the pendulum's center of gravity fractionally, speeding the swing by 0.4 seconds per day. Removing a penny slows it. The clock keeper adds or removes pennies based on daily comparison with atomic time, maintaining accuracy within one second per day.

faq.question: Has Big Ben's bell ever cracked?
faq.answer: Yes, twice. The first bell cracked during testing in 1857 and was recast. The replacement cracked in 1859 shortly after installation. Rather than recast again, the bell was rotated so the hammer strikes a different spot. The crack gives Big Ben its distinctive slightly imperfect tone.
